analysis.one_liner: Restricts bank overdraft fees: requires customer consent, caps how often fees can be charged, and bans fees on declined debit transactions.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after a November 2009 Senate Banking Committee hearing, it sat in committee and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the rules for overdraft programs, the service that covers a purchase when a checking account is short and then charges a fee for it. Banks could only charge an overdraft fee on an ATM withdrawal or debit card purchase if the customer first agreed to the program in writing. They could charge no more than one overdraft fee a month and six a year per account, fees would have to be proportional to the actual cost of processing the transaction, transactions would have to be posted in the order that minimizes fees, and banks could no longer charge a fee for a declined ATM or debit transaction. It also barred banks from punishing customers who opt out and set a one-year freeze on raising overdraft fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Checking account customers who occasionally spend more than their balance, especially low- and moderate-income households who overdraft repeatedly and can rack up multiple fees in a single day. The bill's own findings state that these practices have placed significant financial burdens on low- and moderate-income consumers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Overdrafted low- and moderate-income checking customers

how_it_helps.text: Requires a customer's written or electronic consent before a bank can charge overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals or debit card purchases, so the feature can no longer be quietly applied to every account [S3].
Caps overdraft coverage fees at one per calendar month and six per calendar year per account, ending the practice of stacking multiple fees in a single day [S3].
Requires fees to be reasonable and proportional to the cost of processing the transaction, and requires banks to post transactions in the order that minimizes avoidable fees [S3].

Bans overdraft fees when an overdraft results only from a merchant's temporary hold exceeding the actual purchase amount, and bans non-sufficient funds fees on declined ATM and debit card transactions [S3].

Requires real-time notice when an overdraft happens, warnings before a teller or ATM transaction would trigger a fee with a chance to cancel, and bars banks from denying account terms to customers who opt out [S3].

Bars banks from raising overdraft fees during a one-year moratorium after enactment and from reporting overdraft use to consumer reporting agencies when the overdraft is repaid under the program's terms [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Depository institutions: banks, thrifts, and credit unions, whose overdraft fee income is a major revenue line. Some might respond by tightening free-checking terms or declining to pay overdrafts beyond the fee cap.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks and credit unions earning overdraft fees

drawbacks.text: Banks and credit unions could lose a substantial revenue stream, and smaller institutions in particular may raise other account fees, tighten free checking eligibility, or cut other services to make up the difference.

By capping how often a bank can charge for covering an overdraft, the bill gives banks an incentive to simply decline the overdraft instead, which can mean bounced checks, returned-payment charges from merchants, or utility late fees that fall on the customer rather than the bank.

The compliance and disclosure requirements fall on all depository institutions, including small community banks and credit unions that were not the main targets of the stacked-fee practices the bill describes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and targeted at the customers the bill's own findings describe as harmed: people charged multiple flat fees for small transactions they did not knowingly agree to. The costs are real but largely borne by the institutions, with a plausible spillover in the form of banks declining overdrafts more often, which shifts some risk back onto customers in the form of bounced transactions. On balance the bill addresses a documented one-sided fee practice while leaving banks a lawful way to price accounts.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which held a hearing in November 2009 but never approved it, and it died in committee when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Dodd, joined by 10 Democratic cosponsors, introduced the bill on October 19, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S5].
The Banking Committee held a hearing on the bill on November 17, 2009, the only committee action in the bill's history [S5].
No markup was scheduled and no vote ever took place in either chamber; the last action in the record is the November 2009 hearing, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Depository institutions kept charging the existing overdraft fee structure, since the bill never reached a markup or a floor vote in either chamber.

for.role: Cosponsors, including Schumer, Reed, Brown, Levin, Merkley, Menendez, and Reid

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but never brought it to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record to measure the split.

industries.note: Overdraft fees are a large, recurring revenue stream built on charging a flat fee, sometimes several in one day, for covering shortfalls that customers often did not knowingly sign up for; the bill would cap the frequency of those fees, require opt-in consent, and ban fees on declined ATM and debit transactions.
